plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic array of circles arranged in six vertical columns, with arrows drawn among them and part of the field sitting on a gray background. Five columns hold five circles each, evenly stacked from top to bottom, while the rightmost column holds only three. In every full column the circle in the middle position is an open white disk and the remaining circles are filled solid black. The white disk in the third column from the left carries the italic label x. Straight vertical arrows within each full column run upward from lower circles to the middle disk and from that disk to the circle above, and long curved arrows arc from a column's bottom circle to its topmost one. Along the row of white disks, horizontal arrows point inward toward x: the disks in the fourth through sixth columns send arrows leftward into x, with farther ones curving above intervening columns, and x in turn sends arrows leftward to the disks in the second and first columns. A rounded gray region with stepped edges covers the two circles below x in its own column together with the white disk and every circle beneath it in each column to the right. Because each arrow encodes an ordering between two elements, the shaded block gathers the elements the arrow chains place on one side of x, turning a counting argument about the quality of a partition into a visible area.

interactions.label: SELECT proof phase
interactions.teaches: The SELECT partition guarantee is built in layers: first groups of five, then each group median, then the median-of-medians x, and finally the counted elements whose order relative to x is already certified
The shaded elements are counted because comparison chains pass through their group median and then through x; they need not each be compared directly with x

interactions.label: Certified side
interactions.teaches: The same median-of-medians argument gives a symmetric lower bound on both sides of the partition, preventing either side from being too large

demo_steps.title: Group into fives
demo_steps.narration: The elements are arranged as vertical groups of five, with a short final group at the right. At this first phase the learner sees the grouping structure before any counting argument is added.

demo_steps.title: Mark group medians
demo_steps.narration: The middle element of each group is shown as an open circle. These medians summarize each group after the elements inside the group have been ordered.

demo_steps.title: Choose x
demo_steps.narration: The third median is labeled x, the median of the group medians in this schematic. Arrows along the median row show which group medians are known to lie on either side of x.

demo_steps.title: Count known-greater elements
demo_steps.narration: The gray region appears on the source-figure side: elements in groups whose medians are beyond x are counted together with the elements below those medians in the drawing. Clicking x highlights the comparison chains that certify these elements relative to x.

demo_steps.title: Switch to the symmetric side
demo_steps.narration: The shaded block switches to the opposite side of x. The learner sees that the proof gives the same kind of lower bound for elements known to be less than x.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: This is a flat 2D schematic in the XY plane, not a depth scene. Use +X screen-right and +Y screen-up. Circle radius about 0.16 world units. Column x-positions: c1=-3.0, c2=-1.75, c3=-0.5, c4=0.75, c5=2.0, c6=3.25. Full columns c1 through c5 have circles at y=2.25, 1.1, 0, -1.1, -2.25. Rightmost column c6 has circles only at y=1.1, 0, -1.1. In every column, the y=0 circle is an open white disk with black stroke; all other circles are solid black. Label x is italic black, placed just to the lower right of the third-column median, roughly at (-0.28, -0.28). Arrows are black strokes about 0.025 world units wide with filled triangular arrowheads. Vertical arrows lie on each column centerline: from y=-1.1 to y=0 and from y=0 to y=1.1, with arrowheads pointing upward. Long curved arrows in full columns run up the left side of each column from the bottom circle toward the top circle, bowed leftward by about 0.25 units, with arrowheads near y=1.8. Median-row arrows: c3 to c2 is nearly straight horizontal with arrowhead at c2; c3 to c1 is a shallow arc above the median row with arrowhead at c1; c4 to c3 is straight horizontal with arrowhead at c3; c5 to c3 is a shallow arc above c4 with arrowhead at c3; c6 to c3 is a larger arc above c4 and c5 with arrowhead at c3. The gray source-region for 'Known greater than x' should be a light gray #bfbfbf rounded stepped polygon behind the circles and arrows, matching the figure: it covers the lower two positions of c3, the median-and-below positions of c4 and c5, and the median-and-below positions of c6, with a rounded top-right and lower-right corner and a stepped notch near c3. Approximate known-greater polygon bounds: lower block from x=-0.95 to 2.65 and y=-2.75 to -0.55; upper block from x=0.15 to 3.75 and y=-0.55 to 0.65; right protrusion around c6 from x=2.65 to 3.75 and y=-1.75 to 0.65; use large corner radius about 0.25. For 'Known less than x', mirror the shaded idea to the opposite side: cover the upper two positions of c3 and the median-and-above positions of c1 and c2, with comparable rounded stepped geometry. Palette: black #000000, white #ffffff, gray #bfbfbf; highlighted comparison chains should use a bright accent such as orange #ff9900 while retaining black outlines.
interactionPlan.notes: Render as an orthographic, front-facing Three.js scene using circles, quadratic/cubic Bezier curves for arrows, and ShapeGeometry for the rounded stepped shaded region. The proofPhase state should progressively reveal: grouped circles only; then open medians and intra-column comparison arrows; then x label and median-row arrows; then the gray certified region. The partitionSide toggle should only affect the shaded region and the set of chains highlighted after x is clicked. For click interaction, make the x circle and its label the hit target; on click, brighten x, the relevant medians, the shaded-side circles, and the arrow paths that form transitive comparison chains through x.

authoredContext: We now examine a selection algorithm whose running time is O.n/ in the worst case. Like RANDOMIZED-SELECT, the algorithm SELECT finds the desired element by recursively partitioning the input array. Here, however, we guarantee a good split upon partitioning the array. SELECT uses the deterministic partitioning algorithm PARTITION from quicksort (see Section 7.1), but modified to take the element to partition around as an input parameter. The SELECT algorithm determines the ith smallest of an input array of n > 1 distinct elements by executing the following steps. (If n D 1, then SELECT merely returns its only input value as the ith smallest.) 1. Divide the n elements of the input array into bn=5c groups of 5 elements each and at most one group made up of the remaining n mod 5 elements. 2. Find the median of each of the dn=5e groups by first insertion-sorting the elements of each group (of which there are at most 5) and then picking the median from the sorted list of group elements. 3. Use SELECT recursively to find the median x of the dn=5e medians found in step 2. (If there are an even number of medians, then by our convention, x is the lower median.) 4. Partition the input array around the median-of-medians x using the modified version of PARTITION. Let k be one more than the number of elements on the low side of the partition, so that x is the kth smallest element and there are nk elements on the high side of the partition. 5. If i D k, then return x. Otherwise, use SELECT recursively to find the ith smallest element on the low side if i < k, or the .i k/th smallest element on the high side if i > k. To analyze the running time of SELECT, we first determine a lower bound on the number of elements that are greater than the partitioning element x. Figure 9.1 helps us to visualize this bookkeeping.
